title: The Three Languages
paragraphs: An old count once lived in Switzerland. He had an only son, but the boy was stupid and could learn nothing. One day the father said, “Listen, son. Whatever I try, I can’t get anything into your head. You have to leave here. I’m going to hand you over to a famous master, and he can see what he can make of you.” The young man was sent to an unfamiliar town and stayed with the master for a whole year. When the year was up, he came home, and his father asked, “Well, son, what have you learned?” “Father, I’ve learned what dogs are saying when they bark.” “Lord have mercy!” cried the father. “Is that all you’ve learned? I’ll send you to another town, to another master.” The young man was taken there and stayed a year with this master as well. When he returned, his father asked again, “Son, what have you learned?” He answered, “Father, I’ve learned what the birds say.” Then the father flew into a rage. “You hopeless creature! You’ve wasted your precious time and learned nothing. Aren’t you ashamed to show your face to me? I’ll send you to a third master, but if you learn nothing this time either, I’ll no longer be your father.” The young man spent a whole year with the third master too, and when he came home and his father asked, “Son, what have you learned?” he answered, “Dear father, this year I’ve learned what the frogs croak.” At that the father was seized by a furious anger. He jumped up, called his men together, and said, “This fellow is no longer my son. I cast him out, and I order you to take him into the forest and kill him.” They took him away, but when the moment came to kill him, they couldn’t bring themselves to do it out of pity, and they let him go. They cut the eyes and tongue out of a deer so they could bring them to the old man as proof.

The young man wandered on, and after a while he came to a fortress and asked for a bed for the night. “Yes,” said the lord of the castle, “if you’re willing to spend the night down there in the old tower, go ahead. But I warn you, your life will be at risk. It’s full of wild dogs that bark and howl without ever stopping, and at certain hours we have to hand them a man, whom they devour on the spot.” The whole region was in grief and terror because of these dogs, and yet nobody could do anything to end it. The young man, however, felt no fear. He said, “Just let me go down to the barking dogs, and give me something to throw to them. They won’t do me any harm.” Since he insisted on it, they gave him some food for the wild beasts and took him down to the tower. When he went inside, the dogs didn’t bark at him. They wagged their tails around him quite in a friendly way, ate what he put in front of them, and didn’t harm a single hair on his head. The next morning, to everyone’s amazement, he came out again safe and unhurt, and he told the lord of the castle, “The dogs have told me, in their own language, why they live there and bring misfortune on the land. They’re under a spell, and they have to guard a great treasure that lies deep in the tower. They can’t rest until it’s taken away, and from their talk I’ve also learned how that can be done.” Everyone who heard this was overjoyed, and the lord of the castle said he would adopt him as his son if he succeeded. He went down again, and since he knew what he had to do, he did it thoroughly and carried out a chest full of gold. After that, the howling of the wild dogs was never heard again. They had vanished, and the land was rid of its trouble.

Some time later he got it into his head to travel to Rome. On the way he passed a marsh where a number of frogs sat croaking. He listened to them, and when he understood what they were saying, he became very thoughtful and sad. At last he reached Rome. The Pope had just died, and the cardinals were deeply divided over whom to appoint in his place. In the end they agreed that the man chosen as pope should be marked by some divine and miraculous sign. Just as they decided this, the young count walked into the church, and suddenly two snow-white doves flew onto his shoulders and stayed there. The churchmen saw in this the sign from above and asked him right then and there whether he would be pope. He was unsure and didn’t know whether he deserved it, but the doves urged him on, and finally he said yes. Then he was anointed and consecrated, and so what he had heard from the frogs on his way, which had troubled him so much, came true: he was to be His Holiness the Pope. Then he had to sing a mass and didn’t know a single word of it, but the two doves kept sitting on his shoulders and told him all of it in his ear.
